title: Copilot was bamboozled into revealing how to hack itself, security researchers claim: 'Copilot wasn’t breached; it was played'
summary: I'm dying over here.
body: There's something really grating about Copilot's cheery demeanour. It's so eager to please, so happy to help, that I simply don't respect it. However, even I feel sorry for the AI tool after learning that security researchers managed to hoodwink it into revealing details of how to hack itself—all by keeping the AI talking long enough until it made a critical mistake. The cybersecurity folks over at Varonis Threat Labs have written a blog post identifying a now-fixed vulnerability in Copilot, dubbed "CoSnitch" (via The Register ). Essentially, Copilot was so eager to respond to technical queries, it could eventually be forced into revealing details about itself that really should be kept quiet. The team began by asking Copilot how to execute an automatic prompt without user interaction, to which it responded that user intent is required, and that prompts cannot be enacted on their own. However, the researchers didn't accept the answer, and kept responding to every refusal with a follow up question. Each time, Copilot came up with a different technical justification to its response—which allowed the team to slowly map its internal architecture, narrowing their focus as they went. (I…

title: Take-Two's former AI guy is, in a twist, skeptical about AI now: 'The guy should be selling you the gold if he's actually got the gold'
summary: "If any of this sh*t actually did what people are billing it as, they would not be talking about it."
body: Take-Two Interactive, the publisher who oversees studios like Rockstar and Gearbox, had an AI guy. 'Had' being the operative word, seeing as he, and a decent chunk of its then-AI team, were laid off around a year after he took on the role. Dicken was previously a data scientist at Zynga, before becoming its director of applied AI in 2019, when a lot of generative AI and LLM technology was still in its infancy. As someone who was the head of AI for one of the biggest videogame publishers on the planet, capable of making such tectonic swings that other developers are scampering to get out of its videogame's launch date, you'd think that Dicken would be one of the true believer types. It's my pleasure to, via an in-depth interview from The Side Quest , reveal that Dicken is actually overall pretty skeptical. It's not as if he's given up on the technology entirely—but he certainly speaks with the same echo as many industry skeptics, including (perhaps tellingly) Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick himself . title: AngryMiao AM Infinity.97 mouse review
summary: Flagship speed, boutique flair.
body: 2026 is shaping up to be an immense year for high-end gaming mice, with everything from the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike to the Razer Viper V4 Pro and the Corsair Sabre V2 Pro proving genuine innovation, with everything from materials to speed and potency all covered off. So when the AngryMiao AM Infinity.97 came across my desk promising a sub-50 g weight with a 30,000 DPI sensor, 8000 Hz wireless polling and some very innovative battery tech, it definitely piqued my interest. AngryMiao is a brand I associate more with its keyboards than mice, with it having a penchant for the weird and wacky, opting for sci-fi-type designs in a similar vein to Gravastar. The AM Infinity.97 doesn't deviate from that formula, opting for a very holey chassis with an aggressive look all in the name of both lightness and standing out from a very crowded ultralight mouse market. title: Acer Predator Helios NEO 16S AI review
summary: A tale of two chippies as cursed power delivery strikes again.
body: I do love a good puzzle. There's something real satisfying about looking at the benchmark results and specs of two different laptops and coming to a crisp, neat conclusion on why one, that's so similar on paper, performs so differently to another. That's great and all, but the fact that that fact is even a thing is a problem. The fact that we're talking about that fact here right now, as a thing, with Acer's latest Predator Helios Neo is a problem. And it shouldn't be. Because you should be able to look at any laptop, see a GPU name, and know what performance you're getting, straight away. It shouldn't be ambiguous. You shouldn't have to dive into reviews, and you shouldn't need to go hunting around in the murky deep waters of spec manuals, trying to find out exactly if this new RTX 5080 is only as good as an RTX 5060, or secretly an RTX 5090 pretending to be an RTX 5070. And yet here we are. Same problem. Different day. But interestingly, it's not just the wattage caps that are entirely the bloody issue for once (like they almost always are). title: Former PlayStation boss Shuhei Yoshida told Clair Obscur devs to not call it a 'turn-based RPG' so people wouldn't 'overlook' it
summary: More than eight million copies sold suggests he might've been right.
body: According to former PlayStation boss Shuhei Yoshida, turn-based RPGs, particularly JRPGs, were so unpopular several years ago that he would tell indie developers to avoid using the term altogether in their marketing—even for a game like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Yoshida recalled giving the Clair Obscur developers this advice during a lecture at the Busan Indie Connect Festival 2026 (via Automaton ). He was impressed by a demo he played a couple of years before the game was out, particularly its similarities to The Legend of Dragoon, a game he produced, but recommended the developers at Sandfall Interactive find alternative ways to describe its combat. "It's incredibly well-made, but it would be better not to call it a turn-based RPG," he said. "That alone might cause players to overlook it." Sandfall listened and started describing Clair Obscur's combat as "reactive turn-based battles" in its marketing. It's hard to tell if that actually had an impact on the breakout success of the game, but it probably didn't hurt. Even if you set aside the supposed genre stigma, I think calling Clair Obscur a turn-based RPG does undercut how active the combat actually feels. It isn't the kind…

title: The Quake shareware CD-ROM contained encrypted copies of every id Software game—and yes, it was cracked 39 days after release
summary: I blame those pesky kids.
body: Remember CD-ROMs? Those were the days, ey? You had to put a spinning disc in the front of your PC to install the games you physically bought and paid for. Actually, in the case of the Quake shareware CD-ROM, it was stuffed full of games you didn't buy, too. That's according to Fabien Sanglard, who's written a blog post on the curious case of the Quake shareware CD release . The game itself took up a mere 22 MB of a CD-ROM's 640 MB capacity, leading John Carmack to joke that if there was ever a CD version of Doom, it would come with a "Making of Doom" feature film to use up the entire capacity. However, it was decided that all that extra space could be put to better use instead—by including locked versions of id Software's entire back catalogue of games. The idea being, you could gain access to the games by calling a hotline, paying for them over the phone, and then putting in an unlock code. Just like you could when unlocking the shareware version of Quake into the full release. In the days before proper digital game distribution (and for many, decent internet connections), this was likely seen as a stroke of genius. However, there was one fatal flaw. Yes, you guessed it. title: Even though turn-based and real time RPGs 'have their loud, vocal advocates,' Fallout developer Tim Cain thinks they both have a place in the genre
summary: A statesmanlike take.
body: In a recent video on his YouTube channel , legendary developer Tim Cain weighed in on one of the great RPG debates: Turn-based, or real time? But Cain doesn't see it as a zero sum game, instead staking out a sensible, radical moderate position on a topic that can prompt forum knife fights. One unique aspect to Cain's perspective: He zoomed out to "real time" period, not just the OG Baldur's Gate-codified "real time with pause " (RTWP) where you can queue up commands to multiple characters while the game is stopped. The specific contrast of turn-based and RTWP is more often the center of debate, given that they have both been ways of digitizing tactical, often tabletop-adapted combat. But Cain doesn't see one style as being inherently superior to another, pause or no pause. He thinks each has pros and cons, and reflects on them more as tools available to devs rather than ends in and of themselves. Regarding real time, Cain argued: It's naturally superior for first person games (excepting very specific edge cases). Combat moves faster, and allows for more characters on-screen without dragging things out. But it's more difficult to control multiple characters, and the "pause" in RTWP…

The premise is simple: you play as Freddie, the owner of a small hair salon in Starfish City, where beastfolk now outnumber humans. So to keep up with the changing clientele Freddie rebrands her shop for beastfolk and snags herself a magical mirror in hopes to beat out the competition who have more money and employees at their disposal. (Image credit: SIGONO INC. ) Any time a client sits down ready to get their haircut you can use the mirror to show them up to three hairstyles they might like. It's up to you to keep track of the options you present them with and their reactions to them and come to a decision of which one is best for them all on your own. title: Intel is keeping Raptor Lake CPUs around for 'years to come' as a cheaper alternative to DDR5-compatible chips

body: If you're running a Raptor Lake-chipped system, congratulations—it seems you're ahead of the curve. Speaking to Tom's Hardware , Intel's vice president and general manager of its enthusiast channel business, Robert Hallock, says that far from putting the 10 nm chips out to pasture, Intel is doubling-down: "Going forward, 10 nm products like Raptor Lake; that is a core part of the portfolio that I want to offer to people for years to come," said the Intel chief. "LGA 1700 is still a good socket. Lots of people [are] still interested in DDR4, so [we’ll] keep offering, and you'll see [pricing] smooth out over time. It'll come back to normal. That's the plan." And it's not difficult to imagine why. While both DDR5 and DDR4 prices have shot to the moon over the past year, it's still possible to pick up a good 32 GB DDR4 kit for around $200 . Not to mention those who want to upgrade their machine while hanging on to their old DDR4 sticks, or pick up a still-very-capable prebuilt PC for less. If pricing and supply can be stabilised, Raptor Lake CPUs may end up being a compelling option once more. title: Intel might be cooking up a budget-friendly handheld chip but I'd still be surprised if it's cheap enough or fast enough to matter
summary: Could this take some of the sting out of the handheld market?
body: Handhelds aren't exactly the most exciting devices right now given just how prohibitively expensive they've become, but you'd better bet my ears perk up a little when I hear of more possible budget-oriented hardware. That's what we could soon have from Intel, if prolific hardware leaker Jaykihn's recent X post is correct. Decoding the string of numbers, according to Jaykihn, Intel will release a Panther Lake chip with four Performance-cores, no Efficient-cores, four low-power Efficient cores, and most crucially, four Xe cores. Ie, four GPU cores. Earlier this year, Intel announced the Arc G3 and G3 Extreme processors, aimed squarely at the handheld market. These scaled back the CPU cores but kept plenty of those juicy Xe GPU cores in there—10 and 12, respectively. Prior to this, to get such Xe cores you had to have, at minimum, the four P-Cores, eight E-Cores, and four LPE-Cores in the Core Ultra X7 358H . The G3 Extreme cut this down to just two P-Cores, and the same number of E-Cores and LPE-Cores. In other words, less CPU grunt but just as much GPU grunt.
